## A representation, not a different differential-equation solver

`KANApproximator` represents an unknown scalar function using learned
univariate edge splines and residual/base functions. It fits into the
ordinary PSM workflow: the dynamics call `p.r(N)`, and an existing solver
estimates the coefficients.

The first backend uses optional FluxKAN cubic layers with fixed grids.
This example deliberately starts with a small, one-edge network; adding
hidden layers is an architectural choice, not an automatic improvement.
The [comparative assessments](../../benchmarks/kan/README.md) include cases
where conventional splines are more accurate or much cheaper.

```{julia}
using PartiallySpecifiedModels
using PartiallySpecifiedModels: solve
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using Lux, FluxKAN
using Random, LinearAlgebra, Statistics
using Plots
default(fmt=:png)
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
```

## Two populations share an unknown density response

We observe two trajectories of the same model from different initial
populations:

$$
\frac{dN_j}{dt}=r(N_j)N_j,\qquad j=1,2.
$$

The synthetic truth is nonlinear in density. The solver does not receive
that formula:

```{julia}
rate_true(N) = 0.9 * (1-N/2) * (1+0.35sin(2N))
truth!(du, u, p, t) = (du .= rate_true.(u) .* u)
times = collect(0.0:0.25:5.0)
initial = [0.2, 0.7]
reference = OrdinaryDiffEq.solve(
    ODEProblem(truth!, initial, (0.0, 5.0)), Tsit5();
    saveat=times, abstol=1e-11, reltol=1e-11)
clean = permutedims(reduce(hcat, [reference(t) for t in times]))
observed = clean + 0.015randn(Random.Xoshiro(41), size(clean))

dynamics!(du, u, p, t) = (du .= p.r.(u) .* u)
```

Each population is an ODE state, but both use the same fitted function.
No trajectory is fitted with its own response.

## Construct and fit the KAN

```{julia}
model = LuxKANLinear(1, 1; grid_size=8, spline_order=3,
                     standalone_spline_scale=false)
kan = KANApproximator(:r, model;
    input_domains=((0.0, 2.4),),
    penalty=:edge_curvature,
    nullspace_penalty=0.0,
    rng_seed=42)

make_problem(a) = PSMProblem(dynamics!, initial, (0.0, 5.0), [a];
    data_times=times, data_values=observed,
    abstol=1e-8, reltol=1e-8)

problem = make_problem(kan)
algorithm = LAML(maxiters=40, jac=:forwarddiff)
fit = solve(problem, algorithm)

(parameters=nparams(kan), weighted_RSS=fit.data_loss,
 smoothing=fit.smoothing_params, EDF=fit.edf,
 stability=fit.convergence.converged,
 stationarity=fit.convergence.stationarity,
 smoothing_advanced=fit.convergence.smoothing_advanced)
```

`input_domains` maps the physical density interval onto the first layer's
logical grid coordinates. The grids remain fixed throughout fitting.
`standalone_spline_scale=false` avoids a separate spline multiplier and
its redundant scaling.

The curvature penalty acts on the **complete edge**: base activation plus
spline, including cross terms. This example leaves the affine component
unpenalized, the API default. A small positive affine penalty is a
statistical prior, not numerical jitter: when LAML scales it jointly with
curvature, it changes the evidence normalization and can favor excessive
smoothing.

Read the diagnostics separately: `converged` means the iteration stopped
changing. It does not establish good fit quality. `smoothing_advanced`
and `stationarity` describe smoothing selection, not global optimality.

```{julia}
trajectory_plot = plot(xlabel="time", ylabel="population", title="Shared density response")
for j in 1:2
    scatter!(trajectory_plot, times, observed[:,j]; label="observed $j", ms=3)
    plot!(trajectory_plot, times, fit.fitted_values[:,j]; label="KAN fit $j", lw=2)
    plot!(trajectory_plot, times, clean[:,j]; label="truth $j", ls=:dash, lw=1)
end
trajectory_plot
```

## Keep a conventional baseline

```{julia}
spline = BSplineApproximator(:r, (0.0, 2.4), 8; initial=N -> 0.5)
spline_fit = solve(make_problem(spline), algorithm)
density_grid = collect(range(max(0.0, minimum(observed)),
                             min(2.4, maximum(observed)), length=100))

plot(density_grid, rate_true.(density_grid); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="per-capita response r(N)",
     title="Recovery over the observed density range", lw=2)
plot!(density_grid, fit.unknown_functions[:r].(density_grid); label="KAN", lw=2)
plot!(density_grid, spline_fit.unknown_functions[:r].(density_grid); label="spline8", lw=2)
```

This is an illustrative fit, not a tuned model-family ranking. The
benchmark studies use separate validation data, repeated seeds and
held-out trajectories; the two curves here are not a substitute for that
assessment.

## Inspect the edge and where it is evaluated

```{julia}
edge = only(kan_edge_curves(kan, fit.parameters.r; npoints=100))
plot(edge.physical_x, edge.base; label="base", ls=:dash,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="edge contribution", title="Complete KAN edge")
plot!(edge.physical_x, edge.spline; label="spline")
plot!(edge.physical_x, edge.total; label="total", lw=2)
```

For this one-edge network, the total edge is also the complete response.
In a composed network it contributes to a hidden activation instead.
The components can offset one another; inspecting only the spline can
misrepresent the fitted function.

```{julia}
exposure = kan_activation_diagnostics(kan, fit.parameters.r, vec(fit.fitted_values))
coverage = only(only(exposure.layers).coverage)
(outside_central_grid=coverage.outside_grid_fraction,
 no_spline_basis=coverage.no_spline_basis_fraction,
 occupied_intervals=coverage.interval_coverage)
```

Leaving the central grid is not the same as losing spline support:
cubic bases extend through padding. Marginal input coverage is not
joint-trajectory support, and neither coverage nor an edge plot proves
that a mechanistic decomposition is uniquely identified.

## Conditional pointwise uncertainty

::: {.callout-warning}
These nominal intervals are not automatically calibrated. The
[fresh-data study](../../benchmarks/kan/FRESH-COVERAGE.md) of this nonlinear
truth and free-affine KAN procedure found average in-range coverage of
about **92% for nominal 95% covariance intervals and 77% for percentile
bootstrap intervals**. The logistic control was close to nominal.
The examples below demonstrate the APIs, not a coverage guarantee.
The earlier jointly penalized affine configuration performed worse;
the [prior investigation](../../benchmarks/kan/UNCERTAINTY-METHODS.md)
explains why this example now uses the default zero affine penalty.
:::

LAML supplies a local parameter covariance. `confidence_band` projects it
through the fixed-grid KAN's parameter gradient using ForwardDiff:

```{julia}
conditional = confidence_band(fit, problem;
    uf_points=Dict(:r => density_grid))[:r]
plot(conditional.points[:,1], conditional.fitted;
     ribbon=(conditional.fitted-conditional.lower,
             conditional.upper-conditional.fitted),
     label="KAN with conditional pointwise interval", fillalpha=0.2,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="r(N)", title="Local covariance uncertainty")
plot!(density_grid, rate_true.(density_grid); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash)
```

These are local, pointwise delta-method intervals, conditional on the
selected smoothing, architecture, fixed grids and fitted solution.
They do not include model selection, prove identifiability, automatically
correct smoothing bias, or guarantee coverage. A multivariate KAN needs
explicit query points rather than an invented rectangular grid.

Without `uf_points`, a unary KAN with an input domain returns a `.grid`;
with explicit points, it returns an owned `.points` matrix, one sample
per row. Here we deliberately evaluate only the observed density range.

## Analytic smoothing-uncertainty correction

For this Gaussian LAML fit, `unconditional=true` adds both the
coefficient-mean and covariance-root terms of Wood, Pya and Saefken's
smoothing-uncertainty correction:

```{julia}
correction = smoothing_covariance_correction(fit, problem)
adjusted = confidence_band(fit, problem; unconditional=true,
    uf_points=Dict(:r => density_grid))[:r]
plot(density_grid, adjusted.lower; fillrange=adjusted.upper,
     label="Smoothing-corrected pointwise interval", fillalpha=0.2, linealpha=0,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="r(N)", title="Analytic smoothing uncertainty")
plot!(density_grid, conditional.lower; label="Conditional limits", c=:grey, ls=:dot)
plot!(density_grid, conditional.upper; label=false, c=:grey, ls=:dot)
plot!(density_grid, adjusted.fitted; label="KAN fit", lw=2)
plot!(density_grid, rate_true.(density_grid); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash)
```

```{julia}
(log_smoothing_variance=only(correction.rho_covariance),
 mean_SE_ratio=mean(adjusted.se ./ conditional.se),
 mean_correction_trace=tr(correction.mean_correction),
 root_correction_trace=tr(correction.root_correction),
 coefficient_step=norm(correction.coefficient_step))
```

The helper's `.covariance` is already scaled. Its profiled-REML curvature
includes the response of the coefficient optimum and profiled scale,
but freezes the final data Jacobian and weights. The coefficient dispersion
is held fixed when differentiating the covariance root. This is a
**local Gaussian working-model approximation**, not full integration over
dispersion, architecture, grids, or a nonlinear ODE likelihood.
It leaves the fitted curve unchanged and does not remove smoothing bias.

There is no silent fallback: unidentified/indefinite smoothing curvature
raises an error. A covariance-only `rho_regularization` must be explicit;
the default is zero. A fixed-lambda refit instead needs a supplied
selection-stage `rho_covariance`. Successful calculation is not a
stationarity, identifiability or coverage guarantee.

## Pointwise bootstrap uncertainty

```{julia}
bands = bootstrap(fit, problem, algorithm;
    nboot=30, uf_points=Dict(:r => density_grid), rng=Random.Xoshiro(141))
x_band = bands.uf_points[:r][:,1]
band = bands.ci_uf[:r]
point = fit.unknown_functions[:r].(x_band)
plot(x_band, band.lower; fillrange=band.upper,
     label="Pointwise bootstrap interval", fillalpha=0.2, linealpha=0,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="r(N)", title="Bootstrap uncertainty")
plot!(x_band, point; label="KAN fit", lw=2)
plot!(x_band, rate_true.(x_band); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash)
```

Thirty replicates keep this tutorial short; use a larger declared
replication budget for scientific intervals. These are pointwise intervals,
not a simultaneous band. Resampling and refitting do not establish correct
coverage under model misspecification, and thinly observed densities remain
weakly identified. The architecture and grids stay fixed across replicates.
LAML reselects smoothing in each refit; a fixed-penalty Adam bootstrap does
not. Both keep the declared initialization rather than sampling network
initializations.

```{julia}
(successful_fits=bands.n_success,
 minimum_usable_replicates=minimum(bands.uf_success[:r]))
```

`uf_success` counts finite evaluations at each point, separately from
successful trajectory fits. Fewer than three usable evaluations yields
NaN interval endpoints and a warning, not an apparent zero-width interval.

## Simultaneous bands have a different target

A pointwise interval concerns one density. A simultaneous band concerns
the **entire selected density grid in a dataset**. Averaging pointwise
coverage across densities does not measure that event.

The conditional covariance version calibrates the maximum standardized
Gaussian/delta deviation:

```{julia}
sim_conditional = confidence_band(fit, problem;
    uf_points=Dict(:r => density_grid), interval=:simultaneous,
    nsim=10_000, rng=Random.Xoshiro(241))[:r]
plot(density_grid, sim_conditional.lower; fillrange=sim_conditional.upper,
     label="Conditional grid-wise band", fillalpha=0.2, linealpha=0,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="r(N)", title="Simultaneous covariance band")
plot!(density_grid, sim_conditional.fitted; label="KAN fit", lw=2)
plot!(density_grid, rate_true.(density_grid); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash)
```

The bootstrap version reuses the complete paired function draws already
computed above. It uses maximum deviations around the original fitted
curve, not separate percentile endpoints at each point:

```{julia}
sim_bootstrap = confidence_band(bands, fit, problem;
    interval=:simultaneous)[:r]
plot(density_grid, sim_bootstrap.lower; fillrange=sim_bootstrap.upper,
     label="Full-refit grid-wise band", fillalpha=0.2, linealpha=0,
     xlabel="density N", ylabel="r(N)", title="Simultaneous bootstrap band")
plot!(density_grid, sim_bootstrap.fitted; label="KAN fit", lw=2)
plot!(density_grid, rate_true.(density_grid); label="truth", c=:black, ls=:dash)
```

```{julia}
(covariance_critical=sim_conditional.critical,
 bootstrap_critical=sim_bootstrap.critical,
 scope=sim_bootstrap.scope, bootstrap_draws=sim_bootstrap.n_draws)
```

These bands are per function and per finite grid, not joint across
different unknown functions or guaranteed over a continuum. Smoothing
uncertainty is a separate issue: the Gaussian calculation above still conditions
on selected smoothing, whereas this bootstrap refits smoothing in every
replicate. To use the analytic correction for a simultaneous band, select
both options:

```{julia}
sim_adjusted = confidence_band(fit, problem; unconditional=true,
    interval=:simultaneous, uf_points=Dict(:r => density_grid),
    nsim=10_000, rng=Random.Xoshiro(241))[:r]
(conditional_critical=sim_conditional.critical,
 corrected_critical=sim_adjusted.critical,
 conditioning=sim_adjusted.conditioning)
```

Do not add the analytic correction to the full-refit bootstrap again.
Thirty bootstrap draws remain illustrative, especially for a
maximum-deviation tail.

The [simultaneous-band assessment](../../benchmarks/kan/SIMULTANEOUS-BANDS.md)
reports whole-grid and pointwise coverage separately and checks grid
refinement without refitting the retained models.

## More inputs and composition

A two-input response can use a composed network:

```{julia}
layer(ni, no) = LuxKANLinear(ni, no; grid_size=3,
    spline_order=3, standalone_spline_scale=false)
interaction = KANApproximator(:g, Lux.Chain(layer(2, 3), layer(3, 1));
    input_domains=((0.0, 3.0), (0.0, 2.5)),
    penalty=:edge_curvature, nullspace_penalty=0.0, rng_seed=42)

g_initial = build_evaluator(interaction, initial_params(interaction))
g_initial(1.0, 0.5)
```

In predator-prey dynamics, call this function as `p.g(N,P)`. A single
two-input KAN layer is additive; composition is needed for general
interactions. A trajectory is a curve through state space, not a filled
surface. Evaluate and report multivariate recovery where the data go.

For a fitted two-input problem, the same uncertainty APIs accept an
`n_points` by two matrix. This template uses a chosen physical state path,
not a full rectangular surface:

```julia
points = hcat(N_path, P_path)
conditional = confidence_band(interaction_fit, interaction_problem;
    uf_points=Dict(:g => points))
resampled = bootstrap(interaction_fit, interaction_problem, algorithm;
    nboot=200, uf_points=Dict(:g => points))
```

The constructed `interaction` above has not been fitted, so no uncertainty
claim is made for it here. Query coordinates can also be supplied for
tensor splines. For single-index and transformed-covariate approximators,
explicit points describe the full response (including inner-parameter
uncertainty), whereas the default grid describes only the outer curve.
The fresh study's scalar composed-KAN screen had poor fitting diagnostics
and unstable interval widths under its declared budget. A larger
architecture therefore needs its own fitting and uncertainty assessment;
composition is not an automatic improvement.

The detailed [multitrajectory](../../benchmarks/kan/MULTIVARIATE-ASSESSMENT.md),
[near-trajectory](../../benchmarks/kan/LOCAL-ASSESSMENT.md) and
[reaction-diffusion](../../benchmarks/kan/REACTION-DIFFUSION-ASSESSMENT.md)
assessments show why architecture, optimizer, support and computational
cost should be considered together.
